reference.source: Clinical genetics and paediatric surgery references
clinicalPearls: Hirschsprung disease is congenital aganglionosis arising from failed craniocaudal migration of vagal neural crest cells, leaving distal bowel without submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) ganglion cells.
In the long-segment form the aganglionosis extends proximal to the rectosigmoid, sometimes involving the entire colon (total colonic aganglionosis).
Long-segment disease is more often familial and shows a stronger association with RET proto-oncogene variants than short-segment disease.
The marked male predominance of short-segment disease is less pronounced, with a more equal sex distribution in the long-segment form.
Neonates present with delayed passage of meconium, abdominal distension and bilious vomiting.
Diagnosis rests on rectal biopsy showing absent ganglion cells, hypertrophied nerve trunks, increased acetylcholinesterase activity and loss of calretinin staining.
Contrast enema is less reliable for locating the transition zone in long-segment and total colonic disease, where colonic calibre can appear deceptively normal.
Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis is the principal life-threatening complication.
reference.pathophysiology: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of the craniocaudal migration, proliferation, differentiation or survival of vagal neural crest-derived cells that form the enteric nervous system, leaving a distal bowel segment devoid of submucosal and myenteric ganglion cells. The aganglionic segment remains tonically contracted because of the loss of inhibitory nitrergic and other enteric neuronal input, with relatively unopposed cholinergic and sympathetic tone, so it fails to relax and produces a functional obstruction with proximal dilatation. In the long-segment form the arrest of neural crest migration occurs earlier in development, so the aganglionosis extends proximal to the rectosigmoid and may involve the entire colon as total colonic aganglionosis. Long-segment disease carries a higher genetic loading, is more frequently familial and is more strongly associated with coding variants of the RET proto-oncogene, which encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase central to enteric neural crest development; this contrasts with the predominantly short-segment, more sporadic pattern seen with lower genetic burden.
additionalDifferentials: Meconium ileus or meconium plug syndrome and cystic fibrosis
Megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome and other pseudo-obstruction (ganglia present)
Small left colon syndrome in the infant of a diabetic mother
additionalInvestigations: Rectal suction or full-thickness biopsy for ganglion cells, which is diagnostic
Contrast enema, interpreted cautiously in extensive disease
Anorectal manometry to assess the rectoanal inhibitory reflex
RET and associated gene testing, especially in familial or syndromic cases
Intraoperative seromuscular mapping biopsies to define the proximal extent of aganglionosis
Screening for associated conditions such as Down syndrome, RET-related MEN2A and Waardenburg-Shah features
redFlags: Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis with fever, explosive foul-smelling diarrhoea, distension and sepsis
Delayed meconium passage with bilious vomiting and distension in a neonate
Signs of bowel perforation or toxic megacolon
Failure to thrive with persistent abdominal distension
Syndromic features or a family history implying higher genetic risk
reference.prognosis: After a correctly performed pull-through most children achieve acceptable continence, but long-segment and total colonic disease carry higher rates of persistent bowel dysfunction, faecal incontinence or constipation and recurrent enterocolitis than short-segment disease. Enterocolitis remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Relying on the contrast-enema transition zone, which is unreliable in long-segment and total colonic disease
Failing to recognise and urgently treat enterocolitis
Inadequate proximal mapping biopsies leading to pull-through of aganglionic bowel and persistent obstruction
Dismissing symptoms as functional constipation and delaying diagnosis
Missing associated syndromes with important implications, such as RET-related MEN2A
